title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact, and the balance sheet is where the two are made to shake hands.
epigraph.author: Underwriting Rule, Forensic Desk (house maxim)

web_blocks.html: This chapter audits the numbers behind every other chapter. We work from three records that disagree in small, instructive ways. The first is the audited annual reports for FY24, FY25 and FY26, all signed by Walker Chandiok & Co LLP [1, 16, 15]. The second is the Screener.in ten-year consolidated tables, reproduced below from our blind snapshot [76]. The third is what management told the earnings calls. Where they differ, the audited figure wins and we say so. Five differences need carrying into the tables. First, the aggregator’s Other Income line adds exceptional items to ordinary other income. FY26 therefore prints ₹23 Cr against an audited ₹15.6 Cr of other income plus ₹7.6 Cr of net exceptional gains [1]. Second, its Borrowings line adds lease liabilities to bank debt. The move from ₹4 Cr to ₹61 Cr is ₹40.3 Cr of real term loan and ₹20.4 Cr of leases [1]. Third, its EPS divides profit by all 17.1 million shares, including those held by the employee trust. It prints ₹101.26 where audited basic EPS is ₹102.11 [1]. Fourth, its Dividend Payout 0% for FY26 is a declared-for-the-year figure. ₹86.7 Cr of dividend, half of FY26 profit, actually left the company during the year [1]. Fifth, its total assets (₹912 Cr) net deferred tax assets against deferred tax liabilities, whereas the balance sheet shows ₹941.9 Cr [1]. None of these is a red flag. Each is a reason to read the audited note before trusting a screen.

web_blocks.caption: MPS Limited: consolidated profit and loss, FY15 to TTM (Sep 2026), ₹ Cr (aggregator tables; the audited reports prevail where they differ)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue compounded at 11.9% a year from ₹224 Cr in FY15 to ₹768 Cr in FY26. It reached ₹836 Cr on a trailing twelve-month basis. EBITDA rose from ₹81 Cr to ₹236 Cr (TTM ₹279 Cr). Net profit rose from ₹61 Cr to ₹173 Cr (TTM ₹185 Cr). The FY20 margin trough (24%) and the FY21 profit dip (37% tax rate, net profit ₹59 Cr) are the base for the later growth rates.

web_blocks.html: Read the ten years as three acts. In the first act, FY15 to FY18, MPS was a cash-rich, slow-growing content-services business. Revenue crept from ₹224 Cr to ₹267 Cr, about 6% a year. EBITDA margin sat at 32% to 36%. Financial investments were 56% to 64% of the balance sheet, so other income was 15% to 23% of pre-tax profit [76]. In the second act, FY19 to FY21, margin fell to 26%, 24% and 25% as acquired businesses and depreciation came in. Depreciation rose from 3.0% to 5.0% of revenue. The treasury was paid out to shareholders. FY21 net profit slipped to ₹59 Cr with a 37% tax rate [76]. In the third act, FY22 to TTM, the engine re-ran from a lower, cleaner base. From FY21 to FY26 revenue grew 12.7% a year, EBITDA 17.1% and net profit 24.0%. The 24% flatters because FY21 was depressed. The cleaner read is FY23 to FY26: revenue 15.3% a year, EBITDA 14.6% and net profit 16.6%. All are computed from the snapshot [76]. Audited EPS grew 16.3% in FY26, identical to profit growth, because the share count did not move [1]. TTM EBITDA margin of 33.4% is the highest in the table. It includes only two quarters of the post-Unbound cost base, so we treat it as a data point, not a baseline.

web_blocks.caption: Margin bridge, selected years (aggregator tables, % of revenue unless stated)
web_blocks.takeaway: The bridge shows that the margin story is almost entirely an operating-cost story. Total operating costs fell from 74.1% of revenue in FY19 to 69.3% in FY26 (66.6% TTM). Depreciation, interest and tax barely moved from FY23 onwards. Other income was 23.4% of pre-tax profit in FY19 and is now minor (10.0% in FY26 including exceptional items, 2.8% TTM). Reported profit is now overwhelmingly operating profit.
rows: Other income as % of pre-tax profit

web_blocks.caption: Where the operating costs sit: audited split for FY23 to FY26 (% of revenue from operations)
web_blocks.takeaway: Employee cost is the lever that moved margin. It rose from 42.5% of revenue in FY23 to 45.1% in FY25, the AJE and Liberate integration years. It then fell to 41.6% in FY26, even though Unbound joined in February and revenue grew 5.7%. Other expenses went the other way, from 24.2% in FY24 to 27.7% in FY26. Charge the ₹7.0 Cr labour-code cost and the ₹2.1 Cr AJE severance back to EBITDA, and FY26 margin is 29.5% rather than 30.7%. That is still half a point above FY25.
rows: Ordinary other income as % of pre-tax profit
Net exceptional gain as % of pre-tax profit

web_blocks.html: Three cross-checks on the bridge. First, the aggregator’s FY26 operating profit of ₹236 Cr equals management’s EBITDA of ₹235.8 Cr (30.7%). So the aggregator’s EBITDA is clean of other income and exceptional items [1]. Second, employee cost fell 2.4% in absolute terms, from ₹328.0 Cr to ₹320.0 Cr, while revenue rose 5.7%. Management attributes this to the cost reset in Corporate Learning (segment headcount down roughly a third), the AJE restructuring and AI-enabled production [1, 17, 25]. We accept the direction. But the labour-code charge (₹7.0 Cr) and AJE severance (₹2.1 Cr) were taken below EBITDA as exceptional, which flatters the reported margin by 1.2 points. The labour-code effect is a recurring higher gratuity and leave-encashment cost from here, not a one-off [1, 77]. Third, other expenses rose from 25.9% to 27.7% of revenue. Communication costs grew from ₹19.5 Cr to ₹24.7 Cr. Outsourcing grew from ₹104.1 Cr to ₹114.2 Cr. Rent grew from ₹1.5 Cr to ₹3.6 Cr. Royalty expense grew from ₹0.3 Cr to ₹6.3 Cr [1]. The annual report does not explain the twenty-fold royalty jump, so we flag it for the earnings-quality watchlist. FY26’s 1.7-point margin gain came from people cost, partly handed back through other expenses.

web_blocks.caption: The layer below EBITDA: audited other income and exceptional items, FY25 vs FY26 (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Only ₹4.9 Cr of FY26 other income (32%) is treasury income: bank interest, tax-refund interest and mutual-fund gains. The rest is liability write-backs (₹6.4 Cr), fair-value gains on the put-option liability (₹2.4 Cr), foreign exchange (₹0.5 Cr) and miscellaneous items. The exceptional layer carried ₹29.7 Cr of gains against ₹22.0 Cr of charges. The net ₹7.6 Cr gain hides a ₹13.95 Cr customer-advance write-back that rests on a policy change.

web_blocks.html: Two stories sit in that table. The first is Liberate. MPS agreed consideration of ₹48.1 Cr (including contingent consideration) for 65% of the Australian group in FY24. It booked a put-and-call option for the remaining 35% as a liability of AUD 4.14 million (₹22.3 Cr). The remaining stake was bought on 28 October 2025 for ₹5.1 Cr. The unused liabilities were then released: ₹5.9 Cr of deferred consideration on the first 65% in FY25 and ₹15.7 Cr of the put-option liability in FY26 [15, 1]. The same year the group impaired ₹12.9 Cr of Liberate goodwill. Gains and impairment are mirror images of one disappointing acquisition, so the honest reading is the net, not either line. The CFO told the Q2 FY26 call: “On a going-forward basis, this is a one-off. This is treated as an exceptional item because it’s a one-time entry.” (CFO Prarthana Agarwal, Q2 FY26) [17]. The Q1 FY27 call then confirmed there were “no exceptional items in the quarter” [25]. The second story is AJE. ₹13.95 Cr of customer advances in the B2C author-services business was written back. Management changed its policy to align with market conditions and revised commercial terms [1]. We do not call this wrong, and the audited contract-liability reconciliation shows it (reversals of ₹16.0 Cr against ₹3.5 Cr in FY25). But it is 6.1% of FY26 pre-tax profit and is not repeatable at that size.

That also settles the question the quarterly table raises. The aggregator shows other income of -₹5 Cr in the December 2025 quarter. It is not a foreign-exchange loss. Audited FY26 foreign-exchange items net to a ₹0.5 Cr gain. The unrealised mark-to-market loss on dollar forwards was ₹3.6 Cr at year end [1]. The aggregator’s other-income row includes exceptional items. The Labour Codes took effect on 21 November 2025, so that quarter carried the ₹7.0 Cr past-service charge plus the balance of AJE severance. That is about ₹8.7 Cr of exceptional charges against ordinary other income of roughly ₹3 Cr to ₹4 Cr [77, 1]. Our reconstruction ties to the year. Q2 FY26 had a net exceptional gain of ₹12.81 Cr, as the CFO described. Q3 was about -₹8.7 Cr and Q4 about +₹3.5 Cr, for a total of ₹7.6 Cr [17, 78]. We have not seen the Q3 quarterly filing, so the split is our arithmetic. The annual total is audited. The practical lesson is to check exceptional items before suspecting currency when a screen shows a negative other-income quarter.

web_blocks.caption: MPS Limited: last thirteen quarters, Sep 2023 to Sep 2026, ₹ Cr (aggregator tables; other income includes exceptional items)
web_blocks.takeaway: Quarterly revenue rose from ₹130 Cr (Sep 2023) to ₹224 Cr (Sep 2026). EBITDA margin rose from 31% to 34%, with the June 2024 quarter (23%) as the AJE-dilution low. Other income swings between -₹5 Cr (Dec 2025) and +₹15 Cr (Sep 2025) because exceptional items are included. Quarterly tax rates range from 20% to 29%.

web_blocks.html: Three features of the quarterly run matter for earnings quality. First, margin has stepped up in stages rather than drifting. It was 23% in June 2024, 27% in June 2025, 33% in March 2026 and 34% in June and September 2026. That fits a cost reset plus the AI-productivity story management tells [76, 2]. Second, profit growth lags EBITDA growth in the first half of FY27. EBITDA rose about 39% (₹154 Cr) but profit after tax only 13% (₹102 Cr against ₹90 Cr). The September 2025 quarter carried the ₹12.8 Cr Liberate gain, and tax rates reverted from 20% to 25% [2, 76]. Management itself said that, set aside that gain, profit before tax grew 23.1% in the quarter and 33.9% in the half [2]. Third, the March 2026 quarter (revenue ₹205 Cr, EBITDA ₹68 Cr) is the first to include Unbound. Unbound contributed ₹11.8 Cr of revenue in its first 49 days. According to the CFO its EBITDA margin was roughly 18.5% to 19% [1, 78]. That is well below the group’s 30%-plus, so Unbound dilutes margin until it is integrated. The first-half FY27 margin of 34.3% shows the dilution is small.

web_blocks.caption: MPS Limited: consolidated cash flow, FY15 to FY26, ₹ Cr (aggregator tables; audited statements agree to within ₹1 Cr for FY24 to FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: Over the ten years FY17 to FY26, cash from operations totalled ₹973 Cr against net profit of ₹972 Cr, a 1.00x conversion. FY26 operating cash flow of ₹197 Cr and free cash flow of ₹188 Cr nearly doubled FY25’s ₹101 Cr and ₹92 Cr. The ₹132 Cr investing outflow in FY26 is mostly the Unbound and Liberate payments. The aggregator’s CFO/EBITDA row is measured before tax (103% in FY26).

web_blocks.caption: Cash conversion scoreboard, FY15 to FY26 (₹ Cr; computed from the snapshot, CFO is after tax)
web_blocks.takeaway: Conversion is high but not smooth. CFO/PAT ranged from 0.64x (FY17) to 1.68x (FY21), with weak years in FY19 (0.71x) and FY25 (0.68x). Cumulatively the ten years FY17 to FY26 convert profit to cash at 1.00x, and CFO is 72% of EBITDA after tax. A single year is noise. The decade is the evidence.

web_blocks.caption: Why FY26 operating cash flow doubled: audited bridge, FY25 vs FY26 (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Of the ₹95.9 Cr rise in operating cash flow, ₹65.0 Cr is the swing in working capital. That was a ₹64.4 Cr drain in FY25 against a ₹0.6 Cr inflow in FY26. The other ₹28.0 Cr is a genuine increase in operating cash flow before working capital. Capital expenditure is tiny, about 1.1% of revenue. Free cash flow after lease payments rose from ₹87.3 Cr to ₹183.6 Cr, or 1.06x profit in FY26 against 0.59x in FY25.

Other liabilities (customer advances, deferred income, statutory dues and other)
Capital expenditure (property, software, intangibles under development)
Free cash flow after leases as multiple of net profit

web_blocks.html: The jump is real, but it is mostly a reversal of a one-time drain, so we do not extrapolate it. In FY25 the company settled liabilities that were unusually high at the March 2024 year end, after an acquisition-heavy FY24. The ‘others’ line within other current liabilities fell from ₹32.5 Cr to ₹0.9 Cr. Employee payables fell from ₹30.2 Cr to ₹12.3 Cr. Contract liabilities were flat at about ₹98 Cr. The annual report does not itemise those balances. In FY26 the same cash-flow lines turned mildly positive [1, 16]. Operating cash flow before working capital was ₹242.9 Cr, which is 103% of EBITDA. Cash taxes were only 20.3% of pre-tax profit (₹46.7 Cr), below the 24.5% book rate [1]. In other words, FY26 was a year with essentially zero working-capital drag. The average drag over FY23 to FY26 was ₹24 Cr a year (₹16.4 Cr, ₹17.0 Cr, ₹64.4 Cr and a ₹0.6 Cr inflow). A growing business also ties up cash. Receivables plus contract assets run at 91 days of revenue, so each extra ₹100 Cr of revenue absorbs about ₹25 Cr before offsetting advances [1, 15]. Management’s own framing is consistent with this. The CEO told the Q1 FY27 call: “The business is throwing out INR15 crores to INR18 crores of cash every month” and “Cash flow is normally fairly similar to PAT.” (Chairman and CEO Rahul Arora, Q1 FY27) [25]. That is ₹180 Cr to ₹216 Cr a year, which brackets FY26’s ₹197 Cr. Our decade-long conversion of 1.00x supports it. The first half of FY27 points the same way. Cash and liquid investments rose from ₹113.75 Cr to ₹163 Cr while ₹40.25 Cr of debt was repaid and no dividend was paid. That is about ₹89.5 Cr of free cash on ₹102 Cr of profit, by our arithmetic and ignoring currency and small items [1, 2].

web_blocks.caption: MPS Limited: working-capital and return ratios, FY15 to FY26 (aggregator definitions)
web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days stayed in a 59 to 78 day band for twelve years (63 in FY26, 59 in FY25, 78 in FY21). Screener’s working-capital days swung from +24 (FY25) to -4 (FY26) and ROCE moved from 17% (FY20) to 41% (FY25) and 39% (FY26). Inventory and payable days are blank because this is a services business.

web_blocks.caption: Customer balances and working capital, audited, 31 March (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Receivable quality is high. Only ₹4.1 Cr, 3.0% of gross receivables, is more than six months past due, and the ₹4.3 Cr credit-loss allowance covers it. What changed in FY26 is the liability side. Customer-funded liabilities rose from ₹98.8 Cr to ₹123.0 Cr, but ₹35.0 Cr of that arrived with Unbound. Excluding Unbound’s acquired balances, our measure of operating working capital would have risen from 25 to 30 days of revenue, not fallen to 11.

web_blocks.html: That table explains the swing in the aggregator’s working-capital days from +24 to -4. When MPS acquires a subscription or advance-billing business, it inherits the customer’s prepayment on the liability side but not the cash. Unbound arrived with ₹35.0 Cr of contract liabilities and ₹16.5 Cr of trade payables. Against these it brought only ₹3.4 Cr of receivables and ₹9.6 Cr of other current assets. That is a net working-capital balance of -₹40.3 Cr, or 19 days of FY26 revenue [1]. The aggregator’s table shows the same pattern in FY24, the year AJE arrived with ₹72.3 Cr of other current liabilities. Working-capital days dropped to -13 and then snapped back to +24 in FY25 [76, 1]. Acquired deferred revenue is borrowed from the future. The cash arrived before MPS owned the business, and the service is delivered afterwards. For a steady subscription renewal book like Unbound (company filings cite about 97% gross retention) the balance renews rather than unwinds [79]. If renewals slipped, the same ₹35 Cr would be recognised as revenue without new cash. At AJE the evidence is mixed. Contract liabilities were flat in FY25 (₹98.2 Cr to ₹98.8 Cr). AJE’s customer advances fell from ₹40.8 Cr to ₹26.2 Cr in FY26, of which ₹14.0 Cr was the write-back rather than a cash outflow [16, 1]. The organic signal is the rise in receivables plus contract assets from 83 to 91 days. Ordinary working-capital absorption is the real FY26 story, not the aggregator’s -4. Management’s reported DSO (51 days at March) falls to 45 at June and 38 at September. Our 63 days uses full-year revenue and includes unbilled receivables. We can reproduce about 51 only by excluding unbilled and annualising the fourth quarter. The CFO’s Q2 FY27 summary: “The earnings are also turning into cash. DSO came down to 38 days from 45 at the end of June.” (CFO Prarthana Agarwal, Q2 FY27) [2].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: cash conversion is a decade statistic, not a year statistic
paragraphs: Our house habit is to judge cash conversion over at least five years. A single year can be flattered or damaged by what other people prepaid or what you prepaid for them. MPS makes the point cleanly. FY25 looks poor (0.68x of profit) and FY26 looks excellent (1.14x). Together the two years convert 0.90x of profit into cash, while the ten years to FY26 convert 1.00x. The difference between the two years is not performance. It is a ₹64 Cr drain from settling balances left over from an acquisition-heavy FY24, against a flat working-capital year.

So when the aggregator headline says CFO jumped 95%, our reflex is to ask what the other side of the entry was. Here the answer is benign. We found no pull-forward of receipts, no stretched payables (trade payables are only ₹42.7 Cr), no receivable factoring, and capital expenditure of 1.1% of revenue. That is why we trust the decade number more than either year. The residual risk is not that profit is not cash. It is that acquisition accounting and exceptional items sit between profit and cash, which is where the rest of this chapter looks.

web_blocks.caption: MPS Limited: consolidated balance sheet, FY15 to Sep 2026, ₹ Cr (aggregator tables; borrowings include lease liabilities; deferred tax assets are netted against liabilities)
web_blocks.takeaway: Equity capital has been flat at ₹17 Cr. Reserves rose from ₹237 Cr (FY15) to ₹579 Cr (Mar 2026) and ₹686 Cr (Sep 2026). Borrowings of ₹61 Cr in March 2026 are ₹40.3 Cr of term loan plus ₹20.4 Cr of leases. By September 2026 the loan has been repaid and ₹18 Cr is leases only. Fixed assets of ₹540 Cr are 92% goodwill and acquired intangibles.

web_blocks.html: Two structural changes define the balance sheet. The first happened between FY18 and FY21. Financial investments fell from ₹288 Cr to ₹12 Cr as the cash pile was returned to shareholders (₹93 Cr in FY20, ₹156 Cr including a ₹104.6 Cr buyback in FY22) and used for acquisitions [76, 1]. The second is the build-up of goodwill and acquired intangibles. Fixed assets rose from ₹173 Cr in FY23 to ₹388 Cr in FY24 on AJE and Liberate, and to ₹540 Cr in FY26 on Unbound. At 31 March 2026 audited goodwill was ₹376.3 Cr, or 40.0% of total assets of ₹941.9 Cr. Other intangibles were ₹117.8 Cr. Together they are 52.5% of total assets and 83% of the ₹596.3 Cr equity. Tangible net worth (equity less goodwill and intangibles) fell from ₹162.1 Cr to ₹102.2 Cr during the year, even though profit was ₹173.2 Cr. Goodwill and intangibles grew by ₹177.8 Cr (Unbound plus ₹21.5 Cr of currency uplift on foreign-currency goodwill), while equity grew by only ₹117.9 Cr after ₹86.7 Cr of dividends [1]. A quarter of the ₹117.9 Cr equity increase (₹29.0 Cr) is the foreign-currency translation reserve, which is non-cash. That is the biggest single reason we prefer cash-flow measures over balance-sheet measures for this company.

web_blocks.caption: Balance-sheet items that matter, audited, 31 March (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: The company is net cash on every measure we can build. Management-defined cash is ₹113.7 Cr against ₹40.3 Cr of bank debt, leaving ₹73.5 Cr net, or ₹53.1 Cr after ₹20.4 Cr of lease liabilities. The balance sheet at March 2026 is less liquid than a year earlier, with a current ratio of 1.45 against 1.97. The gratuity provision rose from ₹2.1 Cr to ₹9.2 Cr (labour code). Current liabilities also hold ₹10.5 Cr of loan instalments, ₹14.3 Cr of deferred consideration and Unbound’s customer prepayments.

web_blocks.caption: Unbound Medicine: acquisition accounting under Ind AS 103 (completed 9 Feb 2026, ₹ Cr unless stated)
web_blocks.takeaway: MPS paid US$16.5 million (₹140.4 Cr). It recognised ₹123.9 Cr of goodwill (88% of the price) and ₹52.3 Cr of identified intangibles. Identifiable net assets were ₹16.5 Cr, after ₹35.0 Cr of customer prepayments. The price is about 2.1 times Unbound’s pro forma annual revenue of ₹67.1 Cr and about 23.6 times its pro forma annual profit after tax of ₹5.9 Cr. The purchase-price allocation is provisional. The audit report notes that MPS used the measurement-period exemption, so the numbers can change until February 2027.

web_blocks.html: How it was funded matters as much as what was paid. On 30 January 2026 MPS North America LLC signed the Stock Purchase Agreement. On 4 February the company disclosed the funding: internal accruals, inter-company loans of US$4.94 million, an INR 420 million ICICI Bank term loan at 7.85% a year, and a US$9.81 million equity infusion into the US subsidiary [80, 79]. The term loan was ₹42 Cr for four years, linked to the one-month marginal-cost lending rate and secured on current assets and movable fixed assets. Its covenants cover debt-to-EBITDA, debt-to-net-worth and debt-service cover, and the audit report says they were complied with [1]. FY26 interest on it was only ₹0.49 Cr. It stood at ₹40.25 Cr in March and ₹37.63 Cr in June. In the CFO’s words: “In August, we repaid in full the borrowings we took for Unbound Medicine, so we carry zero debt, and we held INR163 crores of cash as on 30th September.” (CFO Prarthana Agarwal, Q2 FY27) [2]. The CEO has positioned this as a template: “We paid about INR70 crores for AJE. AJE earns more than half of that back every year now” and “Unbound is on the same path.” (Chairman and CEO Rahul Arora, Q2 FY27) [2]. For AJE the audited facts are that the price was US$8.4 million (₹69.8 Cr). The provisional goodwill of ₹101.7 Cr was cut 28% to ₹73.0 Cr when the measurement period closed, mostly by recognising a ₹23.6 Cr deferred tax asset [1, 81]. That history says provisional goodwill moves, so a reader should expect Unbound’s ₹123.9 Cr to move too.

web_blocks.caption: FY26 sources and uses of cash, audited (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash flow of ₹196.8 Cr funded ₹130.1 Cr of acquisitions (Unbound net of cash acquired, plus the remaining 35% of Liberate). It also funded ₹86.7 Cr of dividends (the FY25 final of ₹50 a share), capital expenditure and leases. Net new borrowing of ₹40.25 Cr bridged the gap. Cash and equivalents rose ₹12.4 Cr to ₹76.6 Cr, plus ₹0.7 Cr of currency effect.

web_blocks.html: The balance-sheet reading is favourable, with two qualifiers. First the favourable side. Debt-to-equity was 0.07 and the debt-service cover ratio the company reports is 28.9 times. The term loan was fully repaid within six months of drawing. That is the behaviour of a cash-rich buyer using a facility for timing, not leverage [1, 2]. Qualifier one: the capital-structure note says the group has ‘always been a net cash group’. But management has also said it is comfortable with debt well above this level. The CEO told the Q1 FY27 call that an acquisition “in the INR300 crores, INR500 crores range seems fairly doable between internal cash accruals as well as debt”. He added that debt of ₹200 Cr is ‘very comfortable’ against profit of ₹200 Cr (Chairman and CEO Rahul Arora, Q1 FY27) [25]. The near-zero debt balance is a feature of the last two years, not a permanent policy. Qualifier two: lease liabilities rose five-fold to ₹20.4 Cr. That includes ₹19.6 Cr of new leases in the year and ₹3.5 Cr acquired with Unbound. The group also expensed ₹17.1 Cr on short-term leases. So ‘no debt’ understates fixed premises commitments modestly, although at 0.26 times EBITDA (loan plus leases) they are small [1]. Currency is the other structural exposure. 99.5% of revenue is earned abroad. The net dollar balance-sheet exposure was ₹113.9 Cr, and a 1% move changes pre-tax profit by ₹1.1 Cr. The forwards in place covered US$8.1 million (₹74.3 Cr) at an average ₹91.75 per dollar, about 65% of that net exposure. Management says it plans at a deliberately conservative rate and freezes planning rates in two-year cycles [1, 2].

web_blocks.caption: Goodwill by cash-generating unit and the earnings it must justify (audited, 31 March 2026, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Research goodwill (₹119.5 Cr) equals 0.7 times its segment result and Education goodwill (₹156.4 Cr) 2.0 times. Corporate Learning goodwill (₹100.4 Cr) is 8.9 times a segment result that fell 43% to ₹11.3 Cr. That is where the single FY26 impairment (₹12.9 Cr on Liberate) landed. It is the unit to watch.

web_blocks.html: Impairment testing is done annually on value in use, with external fair-value experts. The discount rates are 14.5% to 19% and terminal growth is 1.5% to 4%. The audited note says there would be no impairment even if the cost of capital rose one point and terminal growth fell one point [1]. Walker Chandiok made goodwill impairment a key audit matter in FY26, for the first time in the three reports we read. Liberate was the unit that failed the test [1, 16, 15]. We read the Corporate Learning figures with care. Revenue fell 16.5% to ₹96.0 Cr and segment result fell from ₹20.0 Cr to ₹11.3 Cr. The ₹100.4 Cr of goodwill has not been written down beyond Liberate. In its favour, the segment’s EBITDA margin has been recovering. The Q2 FY27 call put it at about 16% rising to 25% in the first half of FY27, with 19% fewer people. Rodney Beach, the Australian investor who put ₹8.7 Cr into MPS Interactive Systems in October 2025, has become president of the segment [2, 1]. Our judgement is that no further impairment is evident from the audited headroom statement. But a segment earning ₹11 Cr to carry ₹100 Cr of goodwill needs the margin recovery to be real. The FY26 P&L carries a non-cash impairment and a larger non-cash gain on the related liability in the same year. That is why we net the two.

web_blocks.caption: ROCE decomposition: aggregator figure, our simple calculation and the audited note (EBIT = EBITDA less depreciation; capital = equity plus borrowings)
web_blocks.takeaway: Between FY20 and FY25 our simple ROCE rose from 16.6% to 38.2%. Revenue more than doubled (+119%) while capital employed grew only 25%. Asset turns (0.86x to 1.51x) explain about two-thirds of the improvement. EBIT margin (19.3% to 25.3%) explains about one-third. In FY26 asset turns fell back to 1.17x as acquisition capital entered the base with only 50 days of earnings. Every measure we can reproduce is lower in FY26 than FY25.
rows: Financial investments as % of total assets
Audited note: EBIT over average capital employed (incl. leases and deferred tax)

web_blocks.html: Why did ROCE rise from 17% to the high 30s? Not because the business suddenly became capital-light. It already was. The FY19 and FY20 base was depressed by a large cash and investment balance that earned little. Investments were 64% of assets in FY18, 39% in FY19 and 19% in FY20. EBITDA margin was also only 24%. Then the company shrank its capital base through payouts. Net worth went from ₹472 Cr in FY19 to ₹367 Cr in FY20 and FY22, even as revenue rose from ₹332 Cr to ₹449 Cr. Margin recovered, and revenue per rupee of capital rose from 0.86x to 1.51x [76]. FY15’s 49% ROCE sat on a balance sheet that was 56% financial investments, with a 36% EBITDA margin on a ₹224 Cr revenue base. The definitions differ (our measure of the same year is 29.7%). A ROCE earned when more than half the capital is cash is not comparable with today’s. The FY26 picture needs honesty about three versions. The aggregator says 39% (FY25: 41%). The audited ratio note says 35.40% on average capital employed including leases and deferred tax (FY25: 37.09%). The CEO’s letter says 38.2%, ‘sustained even after absorbing the full balance-sheet impact of the Unbound Medicine acquisition’ [1]. We could not reproduce 38.2% from the audited note’s own definition. On the audited basis, ROCE fell about 1.7 points. That is a modest dilution and exactly what an acquisition carried at 125% of its price in goodwill plus intangibles should cause in its first partial year. Trailing-twelve-month EBIT of ₹246 Cr over September 2026 capital of ₹721 Cr gives 34% on our simple basis [76].

web_blocks.caption: Cash returned to shareholders, FY19 to FY26
web_blocks.takeaway: MPS returned ₹651.2 Cr over FY19 to FY25. That is 98.8% of the ₹659 Cr of cumulative net profit and 99.7% of cumulative operating cash flow. It included a buyback (₹104.6 Cr in FY22) alongside dividends. Distribution has been lumpy by design: 31% of profit in FY23, 179% in FY22. Dividends declared for FY26 were nil. Cash paid out in FY26 was ₹86.7 Cr, being the FY25 final of ₹50 per share.
headers: Dividend per share declared for the year
rows: Includes ₹104.6 Cr buyback; share count fell 6%
0% declared (50% of profit paid in cash)
Board recommended no dividend; capital deployed into Unbound
Returned over ₹650 Cr in 7 years per the annual report

web_blocks.html: Dividend policy is the clearest example of an aggregator row hiding the story. The Screener payout of 0% in FY26 and 95% to 108% in FY24 and FY25 is correct on a declared basis. But the cash flow statement shows dividends paid of ₹134.5 Cr in FY25 (90% of that year’s profit) and ₹86.7 Cr in FY26 (50%). The FY25 final of ₹50 a share was paid in September 2025 [1, 16]. The promoter holding company took ₹58.5 Cr of the FY26 outflow (67%) [1]. For FY26 itself, the Directors’ Report states: “the Board of Directors of the Company has not recommended any dividend for the financial year 2025-26”. The CEO’s letter says “We did not pay a final dividend” because “the opportunity was larger than the cash in hand” [1]. Management restated the rule on the Q2 FY27 call: “On capital allocation, our first call this year is growth. And that includes acquisitions... Once that capital is deployed, distributions resume. The principle has held since FY19: capital must earn its return within 12 months, or it goes back to the shareholders.” (Chairman and CEO Rahul Arora, Q2 FY27) [2]. We found no dividend declaration for FY27 as of 13 November 2026. Our judgement is that the policy is real, and the ₹651 Cr record proves it was followed from FY19 to FY25. But it is a ‘residual’ policy, so dividends are a function of acquisition appetite and will stay lumpy. We do not model them as a steady stream.

web_blocks.caption: MPS Limited: shareholding pattern, Dec 2023 to Sep 2026 (%, aggregator tables)
web_blocks.takeaway: The promoter holding company, ADI BPO Services, has held exactly 68.34% in all twelve quarters. Foreign institutions fell from 3.71% to 1.49%, domestic institutions rose from 0.56% to 2.11%, the public holding went from 26.53% to 27.27%, and the number of shareholders rose from 15,737 to 26,333 (peaking at 29,852 in September 2025). The free float is about 31.7%.

web_blocks.html: Dilution is not a concern. The share count has been 17,105,816 since the FY22 buyback. FY21 to FY22 profit rose 47.5% while EPS rose 57.0% because shares fell 6%. The audited reconciliation shows no issue or buyback in FY25 or FY26 [1, 76]. Employee options are small and are met mainly from shares the MPS Employee Welfare Trust bought in the market. There are 158,316 options outstanding under the 2023 scheme (0.93% of shares) and 139,884 shares in the trust (0.82%). A fifth grant of 79,009 options was approved on 4 May 2026 (0.46%). Share-based pay expense was ₹1.04 Cr in FY26, 0.14% of revenue [1]. Chairman and CEO Rahul Arora’s remuneration rose 47% to ₹6.86 Cr (0.9% of revenue, 4.0% of profit). That is notable but not large. Related-party business is also small. Rent and infrastructure charges to the promoter and a KMP-controlled entity totalled ₹3.1 Cr (0.4% of revenue). The security deposit with ADI BPO fell from ₹1.0 Cr to ₹0.83 Cr [1]. The most important governance item is not in the numbers. In July 2025 the Board approved a scheme to merge the promoter’s holding company into MPS, after demerger of its infrastructure-management and investing business. Shareholders approved it on 22 August 2026. The promoter group’s 11,690,615 shares and all institutional votes were in favour, as were 703,540 of the 703,590 votes cast by other public shareholders. The tribunal passed its second-motion order on 16 September and a hearing was listed for 4 November. We have not found the outcome of that hearing [1, 82, 83]. Per reports, the 68.34% block would be cancelled and an equal number of shares issued to ADI BPO’s shareholders. The share count and public shareholders’ percentages should not change [82]. We have not read the independent expert’s report, the fairness opinion or ADI BPO’s own financial statements. The liabilities MPS inherits remain unverified.

web_blocks.caption: Audit, tax and disclosure ledger, FY24 to FY26
web_blocks.takeaway: The auditor’s opinion has been unmodified in all three years, with no emphasis-of-matter paragraph. But every year’s key audit matters include acquisition accounting, and FY26 adds goodwill impairment. The same audit-trail exception has appeared for three consecutive years. The CARO schedule lists ₹36.3 Cr of disputed income-tax demands while the contingent-liability note shows ₹4.0 Cr. We could not reconcile the difference from the text.

web_blocks.html: A mentor’s reading of the audit pages is deliberately blunt. The positive side first. The audit opinion is clean and internal financial controls were reported effective. There were no going-concern doubts and no fraud reported in the CARO statement. There were no delays with statutory dues beyond ‘slight delays in a few cases’, and no covenant breach on the loan [1]. The negatives are pointed, not alarming. First, the audit-trail point. The proviso to Rule 3(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules requires accounting software with an edit log that cannot be disabled, for years beginning on or after 1 April 2023. Auditors report on five points under Rule 11(g) [84]. MPS’s auditor has reported the same exception in FY24, FY25 and FY26. The edit log is not enabled at database level in the main accounting software, and the third-party payroll provider’s assurance report is silent on it [15, 16, 1]. That is a systems fix, not an earnings issue. But three years without the fix is worth a line in the control-environment score. Second, the key audit matters. In each of three years the auditor has spent its most significant effort on purchase-price allocation, a subjective exercise in future cash flows, growth rates and discount rates. In FY26 it added the goodwill impairment test and noted a ₹12.9 Cr charge [1]. Third, the tax disputes. The CARO schedule lists income-tax demands totalling ₹36.3 Cr. Of these, ₹21.8 Cr relates to assessment year 2023-24 and sits before the Assessing Officer. The note on contingent liabilities shows only ₹4.0 Cr. The likeliest explanation is that most of the demand is already provided for or expected to be reversed, but the annual report does not say so [1].

web_blocks.caption: Forensic scorecard: test, result, evidence, grade
web_blocks.takeaway: Ten of the sixteen tests grade A- or better, or B+. The weaker six are acquisition accounting and goodwill headroom, the quality of other income and the exceptional layer, control-environment hygiene, and structural currency exposure. Our overall grade for earnings quality is B+. The cash is strong and the balance sheet clean, but a non-trivial layer of accounting is subjective.

web_blocks.html: What would change our view on earnings quality (business-quality triggers only). First, CFO below 70% of EBITDA for two consecutive years with no acquisition explanation. Second, a second goodwill impairment in Corporate Learning, or an impairment in Research Solutions. Third, net exceptional gains above 5% of pre-tax profit again. Fourth, bank debt above 0.5 times EBITDA for more than two quarters. Fifth, a restated Unbound allocation that cuts goodwill sharply or raises it materially. Sixth, removal of the audit-trail exception, which would be a favourable change. Seventh, a merger scheme that brings unexpected liabilities from the promoter holding company.

Our independent judgement. On the audited record this is a high-quality earnings stream with a layer of subjective accounting on top. The strong parts are verified. There are ten years of 1.00x cash conversion and capital expenditure near 1% of revenue. FY26 free cash flow after leases was ₹183.6 Cr. The share count has not changed since FY22. The loan was repaid within six months, and ₹163 Cr of cash sat against zero bank debt at September 2026. Receivable days fell to 38. The audit opinion is clean with effective internal financial controls [1, 2, 76]. The weak parts are also verified. Other income is lumpy and 41% write-backs. The exceptional layer helped FY26 by ₹7.6 Cr net (₹29.7 Cr gross). A policy change released ₹14.0 Cr of AJE customer advances. The tax rate was 1.5 points lower than FY25. Goodwill and acquired intangibles are 52.5% of assets, and the Corporate Learning unit carries 8.9 times segment result in goodwill. Three versions of ROCE are in circulation, and the same audit-trail exception has appeared for three years [1, 16, 15]. Net, reported FY26 profit of ₹173.2 Cr includes about ₹3.5 Cr from a lower tax rate and ₹7.6 Cr (pre-tax) from exceptional items. Strip the exceptional items, and separately the write-backs and fair-value gains in other income. Underlying pre-tax growth was then between 12.6% and 13.5%, not the 16.3% reported. That is still a good number. We rate earnings quality B+. On the evidence, the cash-flow statement is more reliable than the P&L for this company.

book_paragraphs: Let me tell you how I read a set of accounts, because you will do this for the rest of your investing life and the habit matters more than any single company. I do not start with the profit. I start with three questions. Does the profit turn into cash? What is the balance sheet quietly carrying that the profit and loss does not show? And what has the management actually done with the cash? MPS is a good company to practise on, because it has ten clean years of numbers, three audited annual reports on my desk, and a recent acquisition, Unbound Medicine, that stress-tests every one of those questions at once. I am going to show you where the books are exactly as strong as they look, and where I would put a pencil mark in the margin.

First, the arc. In FY15 MPS had revenue of ₹224 Cr and an operating margin of 36 per cent. Look at what else was on the balance sheet: more than half of everything the company owned was financial investments, treasury, the savings account of a very cash-generative content business. Then the business changed shape. Acquisitions brought lower-margin work, depreciation climbed, the savings account was handed back to shareholders, and by FY20 the margin was 24 per cent and profit was ₹60 Cr. I think of this as a restaurant owner who spends a decade accumulating cash in the till and then reinvests it in new branches that take years to fill their tables. Then the tables fill. From FY21 to FY26 revenue compounded at 12.7 per cent and operating profit at 17.1 per cent; the cleaner measure, FY23 to FY26, is revenue at 15.3 per cent, EBITDA at 14.6 per cent and profit at 16.6 per cent. The share count did not move, so earnings per share grew exactly as profit did, 16.3 per cent in FY26.

Now the margin, and here is the first trick I want you to learn. A company tells you its margin; your job is to ask what has been put to one side. MPS reported an EBITDA of ₹236 Cr, 30.7 per cent of revenue, up from 29.0 per cent. True. But look at where the improvement came from: employee cost fell from 45.1 per cent of revenue to 41.6 per cent, even though revenue grew and a new company was bolted on. Management attributes that to a cost reset in Corporate Learning, restructuring in AJE and AI in production, and the evidence on the calls is consistent with it. Yet the company took the ₹7.0 Cr labour-code gratuity charge and ₹2.1 Cr of severance below the EBITDA line as exceptional items. Put them back and the margin is 29.5 per cent, still better than last year, but half as impressive. When a company moves a cost out of the line you are measuring, put it back before you applaud.

The exceptional layer is where I slowed down. In FY26 MPS booked ₹29.7 Cr of exceptional gains and ₹22.0 Cr of charges, a net gain of ₹7.6 Cr. One gain is the Liberate story. MPS bought 65 per cent of an Australian learning company in FY24 and recorded an option to acquire the other 35 per cent as a liability of about ₹22 Cr. When it finally bought the rest in October 2025 it paid ₹5.1 Cr, so the unused liability was released as a gain of ₹15.7 Cr. That same year it wrote down ₹12.9 Cr of Liberate goodwill. The two entries are mirror images of one disappointing deal, and the only honest way to read them is net. The other gain, ₹14.0 Cr, was a policy change in the AJE business that released customer advances which had gone unused. I am not calling it wrong. I am telling you not to capitalise it, because a one-time accounting release is not a growth rate. The CFO herself said of the Liberate release, “On a going-forward basis, this is a one-off.” That is the right instinct, and the first half of FY27 was clean.

Cash is the question I care about most, and MPS passes the test I trust. Over the ten years to FY26, operating cash flow added up to ₹973 Cr against net profit of ₹972 Cr. That is a one-to-one conversion over a decade. FY26 alone looked extraordinary: operating cash flow of ₹197 Cr, nearly double FY25’s ₹101 Cr. Do not extrapolate it. Of the ₹96 Cr rise, ₹65 Cr is the reversal of a working-capital drain; in FY25 the company settled balances that had been unusually high at the end of an acquisition-heavy FY24, the unexplained ‘others’ in current liabilities and the employee payables, and in FY26 that stopped. What is left is a genuine ₹28 Cr improvement in operating cash flow before working capital and a year with almost no drag. The CEO told the Q1 FY27 call, “The business is throwing out INR15 crores to INR18 crores of cash every month,” and “Cash flow is normally fairly similar to PAT.” I would read that as a fair description of the ordinary run-rate, with growth requiring about twenty-five rupees of working capital for every hundred rupees of new revenue.

Here is the part that confuses people on screens. The aggregator showed working-capital days falling from plus twenty-four to minus four in FY26. It sounds like a triumph. It is an acquisition effect. Imagine a hospital library that buys a subscription business: the new subsidiary arrives with its customers’ annual prepayments sitting on the liability side, thirty-five crore of them, and trade payables of sixteen crore, against only three crore of receivables. The balance sheet suddenly looks like it has negative working capital, but the cash was received before MPS owned the company, and the service will be delivered afterwards. It is borrowed from the future, and for a renewing subscription book it is replenished each year, so it matters only if renewals slip. The aggregator’s table showed the same pattern in FY24, the year AJE arrived, when working-capital days dropped to minus thirteen before snapping back to plus twenty-four. Strip Unbound’s balances out and working capital would have risen from 25 to 30 days. The honest organic signal is that receivables plus contract assets crept from 83 to 91 days of revenue, and that is ordinary growth absorption, not distress. In the first half of FY27 the CFO reports DSO down from 51 to 38 days: “The earnings are also turning into cash.”

The balance sheet is where the headline and the substance diverge most. Borrowings jumped from ₹4 Cr to ₹61 Cr in the aggregator’s table, and one could read that as a company that started borrowing. Open the audited note and it is a ₹42 Cr ICICI Bank term loan drawn on 6 February 2026 to fund the Unbound equity, plus twenty crore of leases. The loan was ₹40.25 Cr at March and was repaid in full in August, with the CFO saying, “we carry zero debt, and we held INR163 crores of cash as on 30th September.” That is the pattern of a rich buyer using a facility to bridge timing, which is how a conservative company behaves. But I do not want you to take away that MPS is a permanent no-debt company. The CEO told investors that an acquisition of ₹300 Cr to ₹500 Cr is doable with internal cash and debt, and that debt of ₹200 Cr is very comfortable. Near-zero debt is a feature of the last two years, not a commandment.

Which brings me to goodwill, because this is where I put my heaviest pencil mark. At March 2026 goodwill was ₹376 Cr, 40 per cent of total assets, and with acquired intangibles it is 52 per cent of assets and 83 per cent of equity. Unbound alone added ₹124 Cr of goodwill and ₹52 Cr of intangibles on a ₹140 Cr price. Goodwill is a promise on a spreadsheet: it says the acquired business will earn enough, for long enough, to justify what you paid above its tangible assets. Walker Chandiok has made acquisition accounting a key audit matter every year for three years, and in FY26 added the impairment test. I looked at which unit carries the weakest promise. Corporate Learning holds ₹100 Cr of goodwill against a segment result of ₹11 Cr, nearly nine times, after a year when revenue fell 16.5 per cent. The Liberate impairment has already been taken. The recovery that management describes, margin from about 16 to 25 per cent in the first half of FY27, is encouraging, but that is the one to watch.

book_callouts.title: Narrator's reflection: cash is a decade statistic
book_callouts.quote: A single year of cash flow tells you who prepaid whom. A decade tells you whether the profit was real.
book_callouts.text: FY25 converted 0.68 times of profit into cash and FY26 converted 1.14 times. Neither number is the story. The two years together convert 0.90 times, and the ten years to FY26 convert exactly 1.00 times. The swing is balances settled after an acquisition-heavy year, not a change in the business. Judge cash conversion over at least five years, and always ask what the other side of the entry was.
bullets: Decade view: operating cash flow of ₹973 Cr against profit of ₹972 Cr, FY17 to FY26.

book_callouts.title: Forensic watchlist for the lead
book_callouts.quote: What the numbers allow you to say, and what they do not.
book_callouts.text: These are the places where the audited numbers rest on a judgement, a reversal, or a disclosure we could not reconcile. None is a misstatement today. Each is where a surprise would appear first.

Corporate Learning carries ₹100.4 Cr of goodwill against a ₹11.3 Cr segment result.

Acquired deferred revenue (Unbound ₹35.0 Cr) flatters working capital on arrival; if renewals slipped, it would be recognised as revenue without new cash.

book_subsections.title: Reading the auditor's pages like a mentor
paragraphs: Most people skip the auditor’s report because it looks like boilerplate. Do not. The three pages that matter are the key audit matters, the exception list, and the Annexure that deals with disputes and defaults. In MPS’s case the verdict is clean: unmodified opinion, no going-concern doubt, no emphasis of matter, internal financial controls reported effective, no fraud noted, no covenant breach on the ICICI loan. That is a good starting position and I want you to say so aloud before you start criticising.

Then read what the auditor chose to spend its effort on. In FY24 it was revenue recognition and the two acquisitions of that year, Liberate and AJE, including the put-and-call option on the remaining Liberate stake. In FY25 it was revenue and the AJE purchase-price allocation. In FY26 it was revenue, the Unbound acquisition, and for the first time goodwill impairment. Three years running, acquisition accounting is where the auditor sees the most judgement. That is not a criticism of the auditor or the company. It is a map of where the subjectivity in the earnings sits.

Two other items deserve a pencil mark. The first is the audit-trail exception. Since April 2023, companies must use accounting software whose edit log cannot be switched off, and auditors must report whether it worked. MPS’s auditor has reported the same exception in FY24, FY25 and FY26: the main accounting software does not log direct changes at database level, and the payroll provider’s assurance report is silent. A systems fix, not an earnings issue, but three years is long enough that I would want it fixed. The second is the tax-dispute schedule: the Annexure lists income-tax demands totalling ₹36.3 Cr, while the contingent-liability note shows ₹4.0 Cr. The most likely explanation is that most of it is provided or expected to be reversed. But it is not explained, and I do not guess about numbers.

book_subsections.title: Returns, dividends and the people in the room
paragraphs: Return on capital employed has risen from 17 per cent in FY20 to the high thirties, and I want you to understand why before you celebrate it. In FY20 the company was carrying a large cash balance that earned little and a 24 per cent margin. Over the next five years it paid the cash out, grew revenue by 119 per cent on a capital base that grew 25 per cent, and recovered margin from 19 to 25 per cent on our measure. About two-thirds of the improvement is capital turnover and one-third is margin. In FY26 the ratio dipped on every audited and reproducible measure, 37.1 per cent to 35.4 per cent in the audited note, because Unbound’s capital arrived with 50 days of earnings. The CEO’s letter quotes 38.2 per cent; I could not reproduce that number and would use the audited 35.4.

Capital allocation has been, in the CEO’s words, “capital must earn its return within 12 months, or it goes back to the shareholders.” The record supports it: ₹651 Cr returned between FY19 and FY25, which is 99 per cent of cumulative profit, including a ₹104.6 Cr buyback in FY22. In FY26 the Board declared no dividend because Unbound consumed the cash. Note two things. The aggregator shows a zero payout, but cash dividends paid in FY26 were ₹86.7 Cr, the FY25 final; and the policy is, by construction, a residual, so dividends will fall when acquisitions rise. Treat the ₹651 Cr as evidence of intent, not a schedule.

On dilution and governance there is little to worry about on the numbers. The share count has been 17.1 million since the FY22 buyback, options outstanding are under one per cent, the employee trust buys shares in the market rather than issuing new ones, and related-party business is ₹3.1 Cr a year. The one structural event to track is the planned merger of the promoter’s holding company, ADI BPO Services, into MPS. The shareholders voted overwhelmingly in favour in August 2026 and the tribunal process is moving; reports say the promoter’s 68.34 per cent will be cancelled and re-issued to ADI BPO’s own shareholders with no change in the count. That should simplify the structure. I would still read the fairness opinion and ADI BPO’s financials before calling it a non-event.

book_subsections.title: Our verdict on earnings quality
paragraphs: Put the strong and the weak side by side. Strong: a decade of one-to-one cash conversion, capital expenditure near one per cent of revenue, free cash flow after leases of ₹183.6 Cr, a stable share count, a loan repaid within six months, ₹163 Cr of cash and no bank debt at September 2026, receivables that are collected, and a clean audit opinion. Weak: ordinary other income that is 41 per cent write-backs, an exceptional layer that helped FY26 by ₹7.6 Cr net and ₹29.7 Cr gross, a policy change releasing ₹14.0 Cr of customer advances, a tax rate 1.5 points lower than last year, goodwill and intangibles at 52 per cent of assets, one segment carrying nine times its result in goodwill, three versions of ROCE in circulation, and an audit-trail exception that has persisted for three years.

Our independent judgement is a B-plus. The cash is real and the balance sheet is genuinely clean; the profit and loss account is slightly more flattering than the cash flow statement, by roughly three rupees in every hundred of pre-tax profit from exceptional gains, plus about one and a half from the lower tax rate. Underlying pre-tax growth in FY26 was nearer thirteen per cent than sixteen, still a good number. If you remember one thing from this chapter it should be this: for MPS, trust the cash flow statement first, the balance sheet second, and the reported profit third, and watch the places where acquisitions send paper gains and paper liabilities through all three.
